source_refs.note: Book p. 102: 6.6 Geometric Mean, definition G/a = b/G, G = ±sqrt(ab), side Note on n G.M.s between a and b

blocks.text:
A number \(G\) is said to be a geometric mean (G.M.) between two numbers \(a\) and \(b\) if \(a, G, b\) are in G.P. Therefore,
\[\dfrac{G}{a} = \dfrac{b}{G}\]
\[\Rightarrow G^{2} = ab\]
\[\Rightarrow G = \pm\sqrt{ab}\]

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: \(G_1, G_2, G_3, \ldots, G_n\) are said to be \(n\) G.M.s between two numbers \(a\) and \(b\) if \(a, G_1, G_2, G_3, \ldots, G_n, b\) are in G.P.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why \(\frac{G}{a} = \frac{b}{G}\)? In a G.P. every term divided by the term before it gives the same number, the common ratio \(r\). In \(a, G, b\): the second term over the first is \(\frac{G}{a}\) and the third over the second is \(\frac{b}{G}\). Both are \(r\), so they are equal. Cross-multiplying gives \(G^{2} = ab\).
Compare with the A.M.: for \(a, A, b\) in A.P. the differences are equal (\(A - a = b - A\)), so \(A = \frac{a+b}{2}\). The A.M. is the 'middle by adding', the G.M. is the 'middle by multiplying'.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Worked illustration (ours): G.M. between \(4\) and \(9\):
\[G^{2} = 4 \times 9 = 36\]
\[G = \pm 6\]
Check: \(4, 6, 9\) has ratio \(\frac{6}{4} = \frac{9}{6} = \frac{3}{2}\), and \(4, -6, 9\) has ratio \(\frac{-6}{4} = \frac{9}{-6} = -\frac{3}{2}\). Both are G.P.s, which is why the book writes \(\pm\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Signs of the G.M.:
1. If \(a\) and \(b\) are both positive (or both negative), \(ab > 0\) and there are two real G.M.s, \(\pm\sqrt{ab}\). When a question says 'the positive G.M.' take \(+\sqrt{ab}\).
2. If \(a\) and \(b\) have opposite signs, \(ab < 0\) and the G.M.s are not real. For example, between \(-1\) and \(9\): \(G^{2} = -9\), so \(G = \pm 3i\), because \(\sqrt{-9} = 3i\) (Unit 1).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Inserting \(n\) G.M.s (used in Example 17): the G.P. \(a, G_1, \ldots, G_n, b\) has \(n + 2\) terms, so \(b\) is the \((n+2)\)th term:
\[b = a\,r^{\,n+1}\]
Solve this for \(r\); then \(G_1 = ar,\ G_2 = ar^{2}, \ldots, G_n = ar^{n}\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(G\) is the G.M. of \(a\) and \(b\) when \(a, G, b\) are in G.P.
2. \(\frac{G}{a} = \frac{b}{G}\), so \(G^{2} = ab\) and \(G = \pm\sqrt{ab}\).
3. Positive numbers: two real G.M.s; 'the positive G.M.' is \(\sqrt{ab}\).
4. \(n\) G.M.s between \(a\) and \(b\): \(a, G_1, \ldots, G_n, b\) is a G.P. of \(n + 2\) terms.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Writing \(G = \frac{a+b}{2}\): that is the A.M., not the G.M.
2. Forgetting the \(\pm\): \(4, -6, 9\) is also a G.P.
3. Counting terms wrongly: with \(n\) G.M.s inserted the last term is the \((n+2)\)th, not the \(n\)th.
